2. Respondent Nos. 1-14 instituted the suit praying for declaration of their raiyati right to the disputed land measuring 29.82 described in the schedule to the plaint, plaintiffs case is that plaintiff No. 1 along with predecessors-in-interest of the plaintiffs 2-14 namely, Jabbar Ali Sheikh, Gagan Ali Sheikh, Hamid Ali Sheikh, Wahed Ali, Abdul Aziz Sheikh, Fajar Ali Sheikh, Sadaruddin Sheikh, Sirjan Ali Sheikh and Meser Ali Sheikh were recorded owners of the lands recorded in LR Khatian Nos. 370, 371 and 345 of Mouza Kapalbhera, PS Galachipa in the district of Patuakhali. Along the east of the said lands flowed the public navigable river Bura Gouranga. Due to diluvion some portion of the lands submerged in the river in 1347-48 BS and remained under water for 12/13 years and then again reformed in situ. The river then receded further towards cast and more lands accreted to the reformed lands. The plaintiffs possess the reformed lands as well as the accreted lands. Sometime in 1963 they applied to the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev) for their recognition as tenants in respect of the said lands under section 86 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The Additional Deputy Commissioner, referred the matter to the Local Circle Officer, (Rev) who claimed the suit lands as accretions to the Government lands and denied the plaintiffs' title to the same. Hence they claimed a total quantity of 29.82 acres of land. They denied that the Government had any possession therein. 

 3. The suit was contested by the defendant Government by filing a written statement contending, inter alia, that the disputed lands were accretions to the Government lands. 

 (2) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, the right, title and interest of the tenant or his successors-in-interest shall be extinguished in such lands or portion thereof, whether the loss of such lands or portion by diluvion took or takes place before or after the commencement of the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Fourth Amendment) Order, 1972. 

 Explanation.—For the purpose of this section, the word "family" shall have the same meaning as in clause (a) of section 151J, as amended by the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Fourth Amendment) Order, 1972. 

 "RIGHT IN LAND GAINED BY ACCESSION FROM RECESS OF RIVER OR SEA. Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force, when any land has been gained by accession, whether from the recess of a river or of the sea, it shall not be considered as an increment to the holding or tenancy to which it. may be thus annexed, but shall vest absolutely in the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and shall be at their disposal." 

 Subsequently, another President's Order being President's Order No. 137 of 1972 was promulgated giving retrospective effect to the said provision and also providing for abatement of all legal proceedings for the assertion of any claim to hold, as an increment to any holding, any land gained from the recess of a river or of the sea pending before any court on the commencement of the order and barring institution of such proceedings in terms similar to those of section 86. By this amending law the provision of section 87 incorporated under PO 72 of 1972 was renumbered as sub-section (I) and two new sub-sections were added. The said two sub-sections run in the following terms : "(2) The provision of sub-section (I) shall apply to all lands so gained whether before or after the 28th June, 1972 but shall not apply to any land so gained before the said date if the right of a Malik to hold such land as an increment to his holding was finally recognised or declared by a competent authority or court before the date of commencement of the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Sixth Amendment) Order, 1972 (PO No. 137 of 1972) under the law then in force). 

 9. Inviting our attention to the present law, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the appellant submits that the suit is hit by sub-section (5) of section 86 and sub-section (3) of section 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. According to him, the plaintiffs, in the instant suit, have put a claim to lands which have appeared as hard soil after the coming into force of Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in the district of Patuakhali where the disputed lands are situated and consequently the suit is liable to abate. 

 10. Mr. Hemayetuddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the respondents, on the other hand, argues that the claim of the plaintiffs relates to lands which have appeared before the coming into force of Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and hence sub-section (5) of section 86 and sub-section (3) of section 87 of the Act have no manner of application to the facts of the case. 

 12. Admittedly Part V of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into force in the area on 5.8.54. The applicability of the above two provisions will, therefore, depend on the determination as to when the disputed lands have appeared after diluvion. Was it before or after the said date? 

 13. On this point the case of the plaintiffs as made out in the plaint is that some of the recorded lands of the plaintiffs diluviated and remained under water for 12/13 years and then as the river Bura Gouranga started gradually receding towards east those lands reformed in situ and as the river receded further more lands accreted to the reformed lands. No specific time was given as to when the lands diluviated and then accreted. It was simply asserted therein that on re-appearance the plaintiffs started possessing the same and some time in 1963 they applied to the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev) for their recognition as tenant in respect of the disputed lands which was, however, refused on the plea that those were accretions to the Government lands. In his evidence as PW 1 plaintiff No. 13 stated that the lands remained under water for 10/12 years after being lost by division in 1347-48 BS. But the plaintiffs specific case in para 10 of the plaint was that the diluviated lands gradually reappeared after having remained under water for 12/13 years. He further said that the diluviated lands, began to reform in situ thereafter and completely reformed within 2 to 4 years and then accretion took place in frontage of the reformed lands. It thus follows that the reformation in situ took place in or about 1957 and then there had been the accretion in frontage of the reformed lands. This witness further categorically admitted in cross-examination that 5/6 years after the reformation in situ they applied to the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev) for their recognition as tenants which was admittedly done in 1963. His statements find support from the evidence of PW 3 who while deposing on 11.11.67 admitted that asali lands began to reform 10/12 years ago which comes to 1956/1957. The evidence of DW 1 is also consistent in this regard. It is in his evidence that the disputed lands appeared in 1362-63 BS i.e. 1956/1957. In view of the evidence discussed herein above we are of the firm view that the disputed reformed lands appeared sometime in 1956-57 and thereafter the accretion took place. It is also found that the plaintiffs were not recognised as tenants by the competent authority. We, therefore, find that the present suit comes within the mischief of sub-section (5) of section 86 as well as sub-section (3) of section 87 of the Act which provide for abatement of all such appeals and suits. In that view of the matter the appeal is clearly liable to abate thereunder.
